title: Throughput SLA Framing and Procurement Script for Dedicated Capacity
body:
Purpose:
This note is a short playbook for sales, solutions, and procurement-facing reps who are configuring and negotiating dedicated capacity deals. Focus: how to frame throughput guarantees, isolation promises, and contract language that procurement teams find acceptable. Includes suggested SLA numbers, tradeoffs, negotiation levers, and a short script for vendor selection reviews.

TL;DR (talking points to memorize):
- We sell predictable inference economics via dedicated GPU pools with isolation and contractual throughput guarantees — not just best-effort endpoints.
- Guarantee: committed throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec) on pinned model versions, backed by availability and latency SLOs; automatic fallback to compatible variants if pinned model is unavailable.
- Security: network and tenant isolation, encryption at rest/in transit, SOC2-ready audit logs and optional customer KMS.
- Procurement win: simplified unit economics, one negotiated performance SLA, and operational playbooks for failure modes.

Target personas and buyer triggers:
- Platform architects: care about throughput determinism and tenancy isolation for multitenant apps.
- Procurement/sourcing: want clear, measurable SLAs and credit formulas for underperformance.
- Security/compliance: want encryption, network isolation, and auditability.
- CTO/VP Eng: wants cost predictability and rollback/fallback policies.

Core positioning pillars (short):
1) Predictability: reserved GPU pools tuned for your workload profiles, not variable noisy-neighbor endpoints.
2) Isolation: tenant- and network-level isolation reduces compliance friction and risk.
3) Measured accountability: concrete SLOs (throughput, p99 latency, availability) and transparent measurement methodology.
4) Operational safety: automatic model-variant fallback, warm cache priming, and observable runbooks for incident response.

Competitive context (how we differ, short notes):
- Generic cloud ML endpoints: give flexible scale but weaker cross-tenant isolation and fewer inference-specific SLOs. Their GPU tenancy is often noisy neighbor and billing complexity makes latency/throughput guarantees impractical.
- API-first LLM vendors: often prioritize model breadth and developer ergonomics; many offer soft commitments but not reserved throughput at scale.
- Self-hosted runtimes: strongest control but highest operational overhead. We bridge the gap: vendor-managed hardware + strong SLAs + integration playbooks to minimize customer's ops burden.

Suggested SLA package (standard proposal to surface to procurement) — negotiable:
- Committed throughput: X token-equivalent/s or Y requests/s for pinned model family (define mapping by model and prompt length). Example: 100k tokens/min sustained with bursts to 120k for 5 minutes.
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for the dedicated pool control plane and inference proxy.
- Latency: p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 600ms for configured sequence lengths under the committed throughput profile.
- Cold-start guarantee: first token served for a non-warmed request within 2.5s for model variants covered by the commitment.
- Measurement window: rolling 30-day window; metrics reported daily and exported to customer SIEM/observability.
- Remedies: Service credits calculated as a percentage of the committed-monthly fee for the dedicated pool: 10% credit for availability drop below 99.95% but >=99.5%, 25% credit for <99.5% but >=99.0%, 50% credit for <99.0%. Credits limited to 100% of monthly committed fee. Latency breach: progressive credits tied to p99 breach frequency (see sample schedule below).

Sample latency credit schedule (illustrative):
- If p99 > 600ms for >72 hours in a 30-day window -> 10% credit.
- If p99 > 900ms for >12 hours -> 25% credit.
- If p99 > 1200ms for >2 hours -> 50% credit.

Isolation commitments (how we describe them):
- Logical isolation: dedicated Kubernetes/cluster-level tenancy for your workloads (no co-located inference containers from other customers in the same pool).
- Network isolation: VPC peering or private link with customer-managed routing; optional air-gapped on-prem package for regulated deployments.
- Storage isolation: dedicated object store prefixes and encryption keys; optional bring-your-own-KMS (BYOK).
- Auditability: per-request logs, access trails, and token-level cost breakdown exported to customer logging systems.

Procurement-ready artifacts to include with proposal:
- 1-page SLA summary (one table: Metric | Target | Measurement | Remedy).
- Throughput definition appendix: mapping between tokens, sequence length assumptions, batching parameters, and model variant equivalencies.
- Incident playbook excerpt: how we triage degraded throughput and the expected timeline for escalations, mitigations, and remediation.
- Security checklist: controls and compliance evidence (SOC2, ISO snippets, KMS integration guide).

Negotiation levers (what we can flex and when):
- Commitment term and volume: longer committed terms -> lower unit price and higher guaranteed throughput headroom.
- Burst allowances: increase short-term burst capacity for a premium or as part of an SLA uplift.
- Warm-cache guarantees: add a cache-warming service to improve cold-starts for time-critical flows.
- Support level: 24x7 on-call SLA with named engineers for enterprise customers at higher tiers.
- Model pinning constraints: multiple pinned model slots vs. single: more slots = higher cost (operational overhead).

Sample negotiation scripts (for procurement call):
- Procurement: 'How do you measure throughput and when do we get credits?'
  Response: 'We define committed throughput using a workload appendix that maps your average sequence length and request mix to a tokens-per-second target. We provide daily metrics and export raw telemetry so you can independently validate. Credits are processed per the SLA table; they are calculated as a fraction of your committed monthly fee tied to the specific metric breach.'

- Procurement: 'We need absolute isolation guarantees. Are other tenants ever on our hardware?'
  Response: 'By default dedicated pools are logically isolated so your inference workloads do not run alongside other customers. For customers requiring the highest assurance we offer physically isolated clusters or our Private deployment where the control plane is separated into your VPC or on-prem bundle.'

- Procurement: 'What happens if you can’t meet the model pins we need due to capacity pressure?'
  Response: 'Our routing tier will fall back to pre-agreed compatible model variants (listed in the appendix) to preserve availability. For major disruptions we will also provide temporary burst credit and post-incident root cause analysis and remediation plan.'

Short ROI framing (two-line soundbites):
- Prediction: Dedicated pools reduce tail-latency incidents by >70% vs run-on-demand endpoints for similar throughput, cutting user-facing errors and improving conversion for latency-sensitive flows.
- Cost: Locking in committed capacity lowers per-token cost and reduces unpredictable egress of cloud compute spend during spikes. We can model expected unit cost vs. over-provisioned self-hosting.

Objection handling (common issues):
- Objection: 'We don’t want to sign long terms.' -> Offer a 3-month pilot with limited commitment, instrumented success metrics, and optional step-up to 12–36 months at pre-agreed rates.
- Objection: 'How do we validate your metrics?' -> Provide telemetry access (read-only dashboards), daily exports, and a one-time third-party verification window on request.
- Objection: 'What about model upgrades?' -> Support pinned versions plus a controlled rollout pathway. We allow staged rollouts and automatic fallback to prior versions if quality regressions are detected.

Contract language highlights to propose (short snippets):
- 'Committed Throughput: Redwood will provide the Customer with the Dedicated Capacity described in Appendix A and measured as tokens-per-second averaged over the measurement window. Failure to meet Committed Throughput shall entitle Customer to Service Credits as specified in Section 4.'
- 'Isolation: Redwood warrants that the Dedicated Capacity will not execute third-party customer inference workloads within the same pool, and will provide evidence of tenancy separation upon Customer request.'
- 'Measurement & Dispute: Metrics will be measured using Redwood’s production telemetry and made available to Customer via daily export. Parties agree to a 15 day review window for disputes.'

Operational playbook excerpt (what we do when throughput drops):
1) Detect via alerting (automated thresholds tied to committed throughput). 2) Immediate mitigation: shift inbound traffic to healthy replica pools and enable burst capacity if configured. 3) Warm cache & prioritized scheduling for customer traffic. 4) Post-incident RCA and preventive mitigation plan with timelines.

Checklist for deal qualification (sales):
- Identify target models and average seq length -> produce throughput appendix.
- Capture peak and sustained QPS/token needs and cadence of spikes.
- Security/compliance gating -> decide between dedicated-hosted vs Private.
- Confirm telemetry export and SLA acceptance criteria with procurement.
- Propose pilot terms and uplift path to long term commit.

Next steps (recommended for sales rep):
1) Run quick workload estimate with Solutions Eng using the customer’s sample prompt set. 2) Produce short appendix with tokens/sec mapping and cost comparison vs on-demand. 3) Send one-page SLA summary and procurement checklist; schedule procurement review.

Appendix: Example metric definitions (concise):
- Committed throughput: the long-term steady-state tokens-per-second capacity guaranteed by Redwood for the customer’s dedicated pool, calculated using the traffic mix and batching profile agreed in writing.
- Availability: percentage of time the control plane and pool proxy are operational and able to accept requests.
- P99 latency: 99th percentile end-to-end token generation latency measured at the ingress proxy for requests within the agreed sequence-length envelope.

Notes and open items for product/legal alignment (internal):
- Finalize default metric buckets and credit caps for standard 12-month deals.
- Align measurement telemetry export format with customer SIEM partners (Splunk, Sumo, Datadog).
- Draft exact wording for isolation warranty (logical vs physical) with Security & Legal.

Author note: This is intentionally a concise, procurement-friendly playbook intended to be adapted to each customer's workload appendix. Keep the SLA summary one page when sharing with procurement; the appendix can be more technical and live with Solutions Eng.

End of doc.
